messages.minimax:
Allow gradient accumulation dtype to differ from model dtype in ZeRO optimizers

When using ZeRO optimization, the gradient accumulation data type was previously required to match the model data type. This change removes that restriction and introduces support for separate gradient accumulation dtypes (bfloat16/float16/float32) independently of the model dtype.

The implementation adds gradient_accumulation_dtype parameter to ZeroStage1And2, ZeroStage3, and MiCS optimizers, with proper handling for type conversion during gradient accumulation and reduction steps. Test coverage is extended to verify all dtype combinations work correctly across ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3.
messages.kimi:
feat: Add gradient accumulation dtype support for ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3

Remove the restriction requiring model dtype and gradient accumulation dtype to be equal when using ZeRO optimization. This change enables mixed-precision training configurations where the model can use one dtype (e.g., fp16/bf16) while gradients are accumulated in a different dtype (e.g., fp32) for improved numerical stability.

The implementation introduces a separate gradient accumulation buffer (`grad_accum`) that maintains gradients in the specified accumulation dtype, while still allowing reduction operations to use the original model dtype. This is particularly beneficial for training large models where fp32 gradient accumulation helps prevent numerical overflow/underflow issues during mixed-precision training.

Key changes:
- Add `gradient_accumulation_dtype` parameter to ZeRO stage 1/2/3 and MiCS optimizers
- Implement dtype conversion during gradient reduction and accumulation
- Support all dtype combinations (fp16, bf16, fp32) across all ZeRO stages
- Update tests to validate the new dtype combinations
messages.claude:
feat: support separate gradient accumulation dtype for ZeRO optimizers

Add support for using a gradient accumulation data type that differs from
the model data type across ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3.

What:
- Remove the NotImplementedError that forced model dtype == grad accum
  dtype for ZeRO, allowing combinations like fp16 model with fp32 grad
  accumulation.
- Thread a new `gradient_accumulation_dtype` argument through the ZeRO
  stage 1/2, stage 3, and MiCS optimizers, sourced from
  `get_data_types()` in `_configure_zero_optimizer` and
  `_return_mics_optimizer`.
- Allocate `grad_partitions_flat_buffer` (stage 3) and the flat
  partition buffers (stage 1/2) using the grad accumulation dtype
  instead of the model dtype.
- Introduce `param.grad_accum` as a separate buffer in stage 1/2 when
  dtypes differ (`use_separate_grad_accum`), with helper methods
  `update_separate_grad_accum`, `set_grad_accum_pointer`,
  `get_gradient_for_reduction`, and `clear_grad_reduc_pointer` to manage
  accumulation, reduction, and cleanup. When dtypes match, grad_accum
  simply points at param.grad.
- Route gradient reduction through `get_gradient_for_reduction` so the
  allreduce operates in the model dtype while accumulation happens in
  the configured accumulation dtype.
- Update the overflow tracker and `get_flat_partition` to check/use
  `grad_accum` rather than `grad`.
- Extend `test_ds_initialize.py` to cover ZeRO-3 and the full cross
  product of model/grad-accum dtype combinations for ZeRO 1/2/3.

Why:
- Previously DeepSpeed required the model dtype and gradient
  accumulation dtype to be equal for ZeRO, raising NotImplementedError
  otherwise. This prevented users from running mixed configurations
  (e.g. fp16 weights with fp32 gradient accumulation) that improve
  numerical stability while keeping model memory low.
- By decoupling the accumulation dtype from the model dtype, users can
  trade a small amount of memory for more precise gradient accumulation,
  which matters for large-model training where fp16 accumulation can
  cause overflow/underflow during gradient reduction across many
  microsteps.
- The change keeps reduction in the communication dtype/model dtype to
  avoid changing cross-rank communication behavior, while accumulating
  locally in the higher-precision dtype, matching the intent expressed by
  the existing bf16-with-fp32-accumulation special case in
  `_do_optimizer_sanity_check`.

[CI] Keep going display on HUD: upload log when test fails (#155371)

I guess this is more of an RFC

Goal:
Enable keep going so that we can get information immediately for failures.  We want be aware of failures as soon as possible, especially on the main branch, this is so that reverts can happen quickly.

Proposal:
A job with `keep-going` will continue through errors in `python run_test.py`.  If a test fails, before it runs the next test, it will upload a fake log that should have enough information in it so that viewing the log will be able to tell you what failed and any stack traces/error logs, and should be able to be parsed by log classifier to get a line.

I am getting the log by concating the test logs in test/test-reports, which is all the text outputted by pytest (unless someone runs with `ci-verbose-test-logs` label).  There are obviously many things this won't catch, ex output outside of run_test.py, some output inside of run_test.py, but it should be enough.

After a log finishes, eventually its raw log is uploaded to ossci-raw-job-status s3 bucket and the log classifier will read it to do classification.  This means we will have to change log classifier to read from this bucket as well.
I'm thinking just add an input parameter to log classifier like https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/6723/files
Also upload the temp results to a temp attribute instead of the real one

To overwrite the conclusion on HUD, I'm thinking a lambda that is s3 put trigger on the fake log being put into s3, that does something similar to log classifier where it just mutates the entry https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/blob/13a990b6787cf19f87cc51381c3f151c6767f2b6/aws/lambda/log-classifier/src/network.rs#L85 to add a new field like "will_fail": true, and also triggers the log classifier to run

Then we change HUD/ClickHouse to point the raw log url to the alternate place, the new "will_fail" field as the conclusion, and the temp log classifier result if needed

Why always write to temp attribution/column? I am unsure about overwriting the real results with fake ones

Pros:
Not many changes outside of HUD/UI

Cons:
Lots of moving parts, lots of temp fields that will require adjustment for queries, temp fields never really get deleted

feat: add Universal Checkpoint conversion and loading support

Add a new `ds_to_universal.py` converter that transforms DeepSpeed 3D-parallel (TP/PP/DP) checkpoints into Universal Checkpoints, enabling users to resume training on a different GPU count. The converter extracts ZeRO shards, merges TP slices (handling replicated, averaged, row-parallel, and vocabulary-padded parameters), and persists the global optimizer state.

Refactor ZeRO stage_1_and_2 to load the global optimizer state from the new `optimizer_state.pt` file via `_load_global_state`, replacing the previous per-rank state extraction path so legacy and universal checkpoints share a common load path. Add the `LOSS_SCALER` and `TP_REPLICATED_PARAMETER_PATTERNS` constants to support the new layout.

In the pipeline engine, switch the BF16 gradient-accumulation gating from `bfloat16_enabled()` to a cached `using_bf16_optimizer` flag, decoupling it from the engine's bf16 setting so PP+BF16 works correctly with ZeRO Stage 1.

Wire `update_lp_params()` into the universal checkpoint load path in `DeepSpeedEngine.load_checkpoint` to refresh low-precision params after loading, and document the new mechanism in `model-checkpointing.rst` pointing to the Megatron-DeepSpeed and BLOOM examples.

feat: Add Universal Checkpoint support for flexible GPU scaling in 3D parallelism

This commit introduces the Universal Checkpoint mechanism to DeepSpeed, enabling users to resume training with different GPU configurations when using ZeRO data parallelism, Tensor parallelism, and Pipeline parallelism together.

The key changes include:
- Added new checkpoint constants (LOSS_SCALER, TP_REPLICATED_PARAMETER_PATTERNS) to support universal checkpoint metadata
- Created ds_to_universal.py conversion tool that extracts ZeRO shards, merges tensor-parallel slices, and reorganizes checkpoint format for cross-GPU compatibility
- Modified checkpoint loading in DeepSpeedEngine to call update_lp_params() when loading universal checkpoints
- Fixed PipelineEngine to properly detect BF16_Optimizer usage instead of relying on bfloat16_enabled() for gradient reduction logic
- Enhanced TiedLayerSpec to support multiple tied weight attributes via tied_weight_attrs parameter
- Updated ZeRO stage 1/2 optimizer to load global state (loss scaler, clip grad, etc.) from universal checkpoint format
- Added documentation for the Universal Checkpoint feature with references to Megatron-DeepSpeed and BLOOM examples

This addresses the limitation where checkpoint reshaping was required when changing GPU counts, making elastic training and hardware utilization more efficient.
messages.minimax:
feat: add Universal Checkpoint support for cross-device training resumption

This commit introduces Universal Checkpoints, enabling training resumption across different GPU configurations by converting DeepSpeed's 3D-parallelism-aware checkpoints to a universal format.

Why:
- ZeRO, Tensor Parallelism (TP), and Pipeline Parallelism (PP) shard model and optimizer states in ways that are tied to specific hardware topologies, making it difficult to resume training on a different number of GPUs
- Universal Checkpoints provide flexibility to change parallelism configuration (TP/PP/DP degrees) when resuming, enabling more efficient use of elastic training hardware
- The new `ds_to_universal.py` tool converts existing DeepSpeed checkpoints to the universal format

How:
- Add `LOSS_SCALER` and `TP_REPLICATED_PARAMETER_PATTERNS` constants for consistent checkpoint key naming
- Implement `ds_to_universal.py` checkpoint converter that extracts ZeRO shards in parallel, merges TP tensor slices, and saves a universal checkpoint format
- Add `update_lp_params()` call when loading universal checkpoints to properly restore low-precision parameter states
- Introduce `using_bf16_optimizer` flag to correctly handle gradient accumulation with BF16 optimizer (replacing `bfloat16_enabled()` checks for pipeline engine)
- Refactor `_load_global_state()` from legacy checkpoint loading to centralize loss scaler and overflow state restoration
- Document the Universal Checkpoint feature in checkpointing docs

feat: Add APIs for modifying ZeRO partitioned parameters and optimizer states

This commit introduces new APIs to enable users to modify fp32 master parameters and optimizer states outside of the regular training loop in ZeRO training. The key additions include:

- `set_full_hp_param` method in stage3.py for setting partitioned optimizer states with proper device handling and synchronization
- `safe_set_full_fp32_param` and `safe_set_full_optimizer_state` utility functions in tensor_fragment.py that work across ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3
- Method binding in mixed_precision_linkage.py to attach `set_full_hp_param` to low-precision parameters
- Comprehensive test coverage in test_zero_tensor_fragment.py validating the new functionality across all ZeRO stages and offload configurations
- Documentation updates in zero3.rst explaining how to use the new routines for modifying partitioned states

The implementation follows the existing pattern of `get_full_hp_param` and related getter functions, providing symmetric setter functionality that handles the complexity of ZeRO partitioning transparently. This enables advanced use cases such as manual parameter initialization, state checkpointing, and custom optimization routines that need to manipulate optimizer states directly.
messages.minimax:
feat: add APIs to modify partitioned fp32 parameters and optimizer states in ZeRO

This commit adds the ability to set (not just get) the partitioned fp32 master parameters and fp32 optimizer states in ZeRO training, which was previously read-only.

Why:
- ZeRO training partitions parameters and optimizer states across GPUs for memory efficiency
- Users previously had no way to modify these partitioned states outside the regular training loop (e.g., zeroing parameters, applying custom perturbations, or implementing gradient checkpointing variants)
- The existing getter APIs (`safe_get_full_fp32_param`, `safe_get_full_optimizer_state`) only allowed reading values, not updating them

Changes:
- Added `set_full_hp_param` in `tensor_fragment.py` and `stage3.py` to write values into partitioned fp32 buffers
- Added `safe_set_full_fp32_param` and `safe_set_full_optimizer_state` as public APIs supporting ZeRO stages 1, 2, 3, and bf16_optimizer
- Linked `set_full_hp_param` to low-precision parameters via `mixed_precision_linkage.py`
- Refactored `_get_fp32_opt_state_partition` to share logic between get and set operations
- Removed unnecessary `.to(device=param.device)` calls in `get_fp32_grad_for_param` and `get_full_hp_param` since partitioning already ensures correct device placement
- Added documentation with usage example in `zero3.rst`
- Added comprehensive tests covering all zero stages and offload devices
messages.claude:
feat: add APIs to modify ZeRO partitioned fp32 parameters and optimizer states

Adds `set_full_hp_param` for ZeRO stage 3 and `safe_set_full_fp32_param` /
`safe_set_full_optimizer_state` public utilities, mirroring the existing
`get_full_*` helpers, so users can overwrite partitioned fp32 master weights
and optimizer states (e.g., `exp_avg`, `exp_avg_sq`) outside the training loop.

What:
- stage3.py: refactor the all-gather path into `_get_fp32_opt_state_partition`
  and add `set_full_hp_param`, which scatters a full tensor back into the
  local partition (handles swappable optimizer subgroups and CPU/NVMe offload).
- tensor_fragment.py / mixed_precision_linkage.py: add `set_full_hp_param`
  for ZeRO 1/2 bf16 params and a `get_hp_fragment` helper to dedupe state lookup.
- utils/__init__.py: export the new `safe_set_*` functions.
- zero3.rst: document the new modification routines with a usage snippet.
- test_zero_tensor_fragment.py: add `TestTensorFragmentUpdate` covering stages
  1/2/3, fp16/bf16/fp32, and none/cpu/nvme offload via set-then-validate round trips.

Why: Previously ZeRO exposed only read access (`safe_get_full_*`) to the
partitioned fp32 states, making it impossible to modify parameters or optimizer
states outside the standard training step (e.g., for custom update schemes,
state initialization, or checkpoint surgery) under ZeRO partitioning. The new
set APIs complete the get/set pair so users can write partitioned states
without manually handling partition boundaries, rank-local slicing, or
optimizer-state swap in/out for offloaded subgroups.

messages.kimi:
fix: Handle empty parameter groups in optimizer configuration

The changes fix a bug where empty parameter groups in client-provided optimizers could cause issues during DeepSpeed initialization. The fix moves the empty parameter group filtering logic to apply uniformly to both client-provided and DeepSpeed-configured optimizers, ensuring consistent behavior regardless of optimizer source. Additionally, the Stage3 ZeRO implementation now properly skips empty parameter groups when building trainable parameter groups, preventing potential runtime errors when some parameter groups have no trainable parameters.
messages.claude:
fix: handle empty parameter groups in optimizer configuration and ZeRO stage3

Move the param_group filtering that removes empty "params" groups out of
the client-optimizer-only branch so it runs for both client-supplied and
DeepSpeed-configured optimizers. Previously the filtering was gated
behind `if client_optimizer is not None`, which meant DeepSpeed-created
optimizers kept empty param groups, leading to failures later in the
pipeline.

Additionally, update `_get_trainable_parameter_groups` in stage3.py to
preserve non-"params" keys (e.g. weight_decay, lr) when building
trainable sub-groups, and to skip groups that become empty after the
requires_grad filter. The previous implementation rebuilt each group
with only an "params" key, silently dropping optimizer hyperparameters
such as weight_decay; and it appended groups with zero trainable
params, which downstream code could not handle.

Add TestEmptyParameterGroup covering both client-optimizer and
DeepSpeed-configured paths, empty weight vs. empty bias groups, and
bf16/fp16/fp32 dtypes to prevent regressions.
messages.minimax:
fix: handle empty parameter groups in optimizer configuration

When optimizer param_groups contain no trainable parameters (e.g., all params have `requires_grad=False`), the training pipeline would fail or produce unexpected results. This change consolidates empty param_group filtering into a single location that applies regardless of whether a client optimizer or DeepSpeed-configured basic optimizer is used, and ensures such groups are skipped entirely rather than added with empty params lists.

[export] Integrate meta kernel generation with draft-export (#150809)

If a custom operator does not contain a fake impl, currently draft-export will use the real-tensor propagation to get an output for the operator and continue tracing. However if we retrace the exported model using `ep.run_decompositions`, or `export`, or run the exported program with fake tensors, we'll still fail because there's no fake impl.

With this PR, after draft-export we will generate an operator profile for each operator call that we encounter, and store this on the report attached to the exported program `ep._report.op_profiles`. Users can then use `torch._library.fake_profile.register_fake_profile` to temporarily generate and register a fake impl based on these operator profiles. This way future fake tensor retracing will work.

The workflow would look something like:
```python
class M(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, a, b):
        res = torch.ops.mylib.foo8(a, b)  # no fake impl
        return res

ep = export(M(), (torch.ones(3, 4), torch.ones(3, 4)) # this fails bc no fake impl
ep = draft_export(M(), (torch.ones(3, 4), torch.ones(3, 4))

ep.run_decompositions()  # this fails bc no fake impl
# this registers fake impls based on the profiles
with torch._library.fake_profile.register_fake_profile(ep._report.op_profiles):
    decomp = ep.run_decompositions()  # this works

new_inp = (
    torch.ones(2, 3, 4),
    torch.ones(2, 3, 4),
)
```

messages.kimi:
feat: Add ZeRO-3 checkpoint loading without optimizer states

This commit introduces support for loading ZeRO-3 checkpoints without loading optimizer states, enabling more flexible model initialization and inference scenarios. The changes include:

1. Add `get_fp32_state_dict_from_zero_checkpoint` import to convert ZeRO checkpoints to FP32 state dicts
2. Introduce `_optimizer_has_ckpt_event_prologue/epilogue` helper methods to safely check for checkpoint event methods on optimizers
3. Add `fetch_z3_params` parameter to `load_module_state_dict` to gather partitioned parameters before loading
4. Modify `load_checkpoint` to use optimizer checkpoint event methods when available instead of relying solely on `zero_optimization_partition_weights()`
5. Update `_load_checkpoint` to extract FP32 state dict from ZeRO checkpoints when optimizer states are not being loaded
6. Pass `dp_process_group` through to parameter offload initialization for proper distributed communication

The rationale for these changes is to support use cases where users want to load only model weights from ZeRO-3 checkpoints (e.g., for inference or fine-tuning with a different optimizer) without requiring the full optimizer state. Previously, loading a ZeRO-3 checkpoint always attempted to load optimizer states, which was unnecessary for inference and caused issues when the optimizer configuration differed. The new `fetch_z3_params` mechanism ensures partitioned parameters are properly gathered before state dict loading, and the helper methods provide safer abstraction over optimizer checkpoint events.
messages.claude:
feat: enable loading module state dict from ZeRO checkpoint without optimizer states

Add support for fetching FP32 parameters directly from a ZeRO checkpoint when loading a module without optimizer states. Previously, load_checkpoint assumed ZeRO optimizer state loading was always desired, which broke use cases where users only want to restore model weights (e.g., for inference or further fine-tuning with a different optimizer configuration).

Key changes:
- load_module_state_dict gains a fetch_z3_params flag that wraps the load in GatheredParameters so partitioned ZeRO-3 params are materialized before state_dict loading
- _load_checkpoint now calls get_fp32_state_dict_from_zero_checkpoint to populate checkpoint['module'] when zero_optimization_partition_weights() is on but load_optimizer_states is False
- load_zero_checkpoint is gated on load_optimizer_states so it no longer runs spuriously during module-only loads
- Replace direct zero_optimization_partition_weights() guards with _optimizer_has_ckpt_event_prologue/_epilogue helpers so checkpoint_event_{prologue,epilogue} are only invoked when the optimizer actually implements them, avoiding AttributeError when self.optimizer is None or lacks these hooks (e.g., non-ZeRO optimizers)
- Pass dp_process_group through parameter_offload/initialize_ds_offload into ParameterOffload so the stage3 engine reads it from a single source of truth, fixing a latent issue where self.dp_process_group was set after parameter_offload initialization
- Pipe engine's load_module_state_dict signature updated to match the new fetch_z3_params parameter

messages.kimi:
feat: Add configurable pin_memory option for ZeRO optimizer CPU offload (#XXXX)

The current ZeRO optimizer implementation automatically enables `pin_memory` for all CPU-offloaded tensors, which can lead to unnecessary memory overhead in scenarios where the training configuration doesn't benefit from pinned memory. This change introduces a configurable `pin_memory` option within the `offload_optimizer_config` parameter, allowing users to explicitly control whether pinned memory should be used during CPU offloading.

The implementation replaces the boolean `cpu_offload` parameter with a more comprehensive `offload_optimizer_config` object that contains device and pin_memory settings. This provides finer-grained control over memory management while maintaining backward compatibility through automatic inference of CPU offload behavior from the configuration.
messages.claude:
feat: replace boolean cpu_offload with structured offload_optimizer_config in ZeRO stage 1/2

Replace the single `cpu_offload: bool` parameter with an `offload_optimizer_config` object that exposes both the offload device and `pin_memory` setting. Previously, CPU offload and pinned-memory behavior were conflated into one boolean, so any CPU offload forced pinned memory allocation (e.g. `get_accelerator().pin_memory(...)` on temp grad buffers and the single gradient partition). This made it impossible to use CPU offload without pinned memory, which is problematic on setups where pinned memory is unavailable or undesirable.

By deriving `self.cpu_offload` from `config.device != OffloadDeviceEnum.none` and introducing a separate `self.cpu_offload_pin_memory` flag, the pin_memory calls in `__init__`, `initialize_optimizer_states`, and `async_accumulate_grad_in_cpu_via_gpu` are now gated on the explicit pin_memory config rather than the offload boolean itself. The `engine.py` call site is updated to pass `self.zero_offload_optimizer()` instead of the legacy `self.zero_cpu_offload()`.

Also clarifies the accelerator-not-detected error message, since the previous "Cannot use fp16 without accelerator" was misleading when bf16 or other low-precision dtypes were in use.
messages.minimax:

fix: Fix ZeRO Stage 1 gradient handling with CPU offload

The changes fix a bug where ZeRO Stage 1 incorrectly handled gradients when CPU offload is enabled. The fix ensures that:

1. BFLOAT16 optimizer type is only returned when CPU offload is NOT enabled (engine.py)
2. `get_gradient_for_reduction()` now safely handles None grad_accum values (stage_1_and_2.py)
3. Gradient reduction now correctly uses `grad_reduc` instead of `param.grad` directly (stage_1_and_2.py)
4. Removed redundant `p.grad_reduc = None` assignments that could interfere with gradient accumulation

These changes prevent crashes and incorrect gradient computation when using ZeRO Stage 1 with CPU offload enabled.
messages.minimax:
fix: correct gradient handling for ZeRO stage 1/2 with CPU offload

- Fix BFLOAT16 return condition to exclude cases with CPU offload enabled
- Fix gradient reduction to use grad_reduc instead of param.grad in independent P/G bucket handling
- Fix get_gradient_for_reduction to handle None grad_accum gracefully
- Fix reduce_ipg_grads to use get_gradient_for_reduction for extra-large param gradient
- Fix backward pass condition to use use_grad_accum_for_reduction instead of use_separate_grad_accum
- Remove stale grad_reduc cleanup in zero_grad and free_grad_in_param_list

These changes address incorrect gradient sources and conditions that could cause wrong gradients or crashes when using ZeRO stage 1/2 with CPU offload or gradient accumulation.
messages.claude:
fix: handle grad_accum None case in ZeRO stage 1/2 gradient reduction

When using ZeRO stage 1/2 with bf16 model dtype and fp32 gradient
accumulation, the engine previously forced the BFLOAT16 code path
whenever the zero stage was 1. This skipped the ZERO_OPTIMIZATION
gradient handling even when zero_cpu_offload() was active, causing
mismatched gradient paths for CPU-offloaded configurations. The check
now also excludes the zero-CPU-offload case so the correct gradient
accumulation logic is selected.

In stage_1_and_2, get_gradient_for_reduction() could return
param.grad_accum.to(dtype) without verifying that grad_accum was
non-None, leading to AttributeError during reduction when the
accumulation buffer had not been populated (e.g., on the first
micro-step or when set_to_none was used). The method now returns None
when grad_accum is None, and the downstream copy_ in
reduce_independent_p_g_buckets_and_remove_grads operates on the
already-computed grad_reduc tensor instead of param.grad, keeping the
reduction source consistent with the buffer assignment.

Additionally, reduce_ipg_grads() for the extra-large param path used
self.extra_large_param_to_reduce.grad directly, bypassing the
grad_accum-for-reduction semantics; it now goes through
get_gradient_for_reduction() so Stage 1 Mode 2 stays consistent.

The backward() condition that gated update_separate_grad_accum vs.
set_grad_accum_pointer was switched from use_separate_grad_accum and
not self.partition_gradients to use_grad_accum_for_reduction, aligning
the update trigger with the actual reduction code path. The stale
p.grad_reduc = None resets in zero_grad() and free_grad_in_param_list()
were removed since grad_reduc is no longer stored as a parameter
attribute.

These together fix a crash and gradient correctness issue observed when
ZeRO stage 1 runs with bf16 weights + fp32 grad accumulation +
CPU offload, where grad_accum could be None at reduction time.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add `exclude_frozen_parameters` option to checkpoint saving

Add a new `exclude_frozen_parameters` parameter to `save_checkpoint()` and `module_state_dict()` methods that allows users to exclude frozen (non-trainable) parameters from checkpoints. This reduces checkpoint size when using parameter freezing techniques like LoRA or partial fine-tuning where frozen parameters don't need to be saved.

The change propagates the new parameter through the checkpoint saving pipeline including MoE and pipeline parallel code paths, and adds comprehensive unit tests to verify both the exclusion behavior and backwards compatibility.
messages.claude:
feat: add option to exclude frozen parameters from checkpoint

What:
- Add `exclude_frozen_parameters` flag to `save_checkpoint`, threaded through
  `module_state_dict`, `_save_checkpoint`, `_save_moe_checkpoint`, and the
  pipeline `save_state_dict` path.
- Filter out parameters with `requires_grad=False` from the saved state_dict,
  and disable `save_frozen_param` for ZeRO partition-gradient mode when
  exclusion is requested.
- Refactor pipeline layer saving to use shared `clone_tensors_for_torch_save`
  helper and add `_get_frozen_parameter_names` for LayerSpec/Module cases.
- Add `test_save_exclude_frozen_weights` unit test covering ZeRO stages 1/2.

Why:
Frozen parameters are constant across training and need not be persisted in
every checkpoint, which bloats storage and slows I/O for large models with
significant frozen backbones (e.g. fine-tuning, PEFT-style setups). Giving
callers an explicit opt-in avoids changing default behavior while letting
them skip redundant frozen weights, shrinking checkpoint size and avoiding
the mismatch where ZeRO's `save_frozen_param` would re-materialize them.
The test guards both the size reduction and the exact trainable-parameter
set contract so the exclusion is verifiable and backwards-compatible (the
default path still includes all parameters).

messages.claude:
feat: add MPS accelerator support for Apple Silicon

Add MPS_Accelerator implementation to enable DeepSpeed to run on Apple
Silicon's Metal Performance Shaders backend, following the same pattern
as the existing CUDA/CPU/XPU accelerators.

What:
- New file accelerator/mps_accelerator.py implementing the
  DeepSpeedAccelerator interface for MPS, including device APIs, RNG
  state management, memory management (empty_cache,
  current_allocated_memory, driver_allocated_memory,
  set_per_process_memory_fraction), and tensor operations.
- Update accelerator/real_accelerator.py to:
  - Recognize "mps" as a valid DS_ACCELERATOR override value, importing
    torch.mps and probing current_allocated_memory() as a proxy for
    availability.
  - Fall back to MPS detection during auto-detect when neither Intel
    XPU nor CPU extensions are present, before defaulting to CUDA.
  - Instantiate MPS_Accelerator when "mps" is selected.
  - Apply minor style cleanup (single to double quotes, spacing after
    comment hashes) in the touched regions.

Why:
- DeepSpeed's accelerator abstraction previously had no backend for
  Apple Silicon, forcing CUDA as the only default on macOS hosts where
  CUDA is unavailable. With PyTorch shipping torch.mps, adding an MPS
  accelerator lets users develop and validate DeepSpeed workflows on
  Apple hardware without a CUDA GPU.
- The auto-detect fallback is placed after the Intel paths so existing
  CPU/XPU users are unaffected; MPS is only selected when torch.mps is
  importable and responsive, mirroring the proxy-availability check
  used for the other backends.
- Unsupported capabilities (streams/events, fp16/bf16, custom tensor
  types, op builders) return None or NotImplementedBuilder rather than
  raising, so the rest of DeepSpeed can import and query the
  accelerator on MPS hosts where those features are not yet available.

fix: Fix ZeRO Stage 3 checkpointing and optimizer parameter handling

This commit fixes several issues in ZeRO Stage 3 optimizer:

1. Fix incorrect partition size reference in assertion error message - changed from `self.partition_size[sub_group_id]` to `self.fp32_partitioned_groups_flat[sub_group_id].numel()` to correctly reflect the actual tensor size being compared.

2. Fix optimizer parameter group management by using `append()` instead of assignment and properly clearing all parameter groups. This prevents issues where parameter groups could be incorrectly overwritten or not fully cleared between operations.

3. Fix test checkpointing comparisons to use correct attribute name `fp32_partitioned_groups_flat` instead of the non-existent `fp32_groups_flat`.

4. Re-enable and fix ZeRO Stage 3 checkpointing tests by:
   - Removing pytest.skip for ZeRO3 tests
   - Updating from deprecated `deepspeed.ScatteredParameters` to `deepspeed.zero.Init()`
   - Adding proper test configurations for ZeRO3 with CPU offload and DeepSpeed Adam optimizer
   - Adding `initial_scale_power` and `wall_clock_breakdown` configuration options for test stability
messages.claude:
fix: enable ZeRO-3 checkpointing tests and fix fp32 optimizer param group handling

What:
- Replace `self.partition_size[sub_group_id]` with `self.fp32_partitioned_groups_flat[sub_group_id].numel()` in the assertion message so it reports the correct partition tensor size.
- Change `_set_fp32_optimizer_param_groups` to append the fp32 partitioned flat group to the existing param group instead of overwriting the list, and rewrite `_clear_fp32_optimizer_param_groups` to clear all param groups generically.
- Update `tests/unit/test_checkpointing.py` to use `fp32_partitioned_groups_flat` (matching the stage3 attribute name), replace the deprecated `deepspeed.ScatteredParameters(zero_modules=True)` context with `deepspeed.zero.Init()`, remove the `pytest.skip` guards that excluded ZeRO-3, add stage-3 + CPU-offload parameter combinations, and enable fp16 initial_scale_power / wall_clock_breakdown.

Why:
ZeRO-3 checkpointing was effectively untested because every stage-3 variant was skipped, which masked two real defects. First, the assertion referenced `self.partition_size[sub_group_id]`, an attribute that does not hold the fp32 partition tensor, producing a misleading diagnostic whenever the check fired. Second, `_set_fp32_optimizer_param_groups` overwrote `params` with a single-element list and `_clear_fp32_optimizer_param_groups` only iterated sub-groups keyed by `sub_group_to_group_id`; this discarded any pre-existing params (e.g. master weights populated during init) and could leave stale entries behind on restore, breaking optimizer state round-trips across save/load. Switching to `append` plus a generic clear of every `param_group` preserves the existing entries and ensures a clean reset. Re-enabling the stage-3 cases with the correct attribute name and the current `deepspeed.zero.Init()` API exercises this path so regressions are caught going forward.

Make torch._chunk_cat support non-contiguous inputs (#151263)

Currently, `torch._chunk_cat` only supports contiguous inputs (due to `.view()` usage in `_pad_chunk()` supporting only contiguous tensor). This doesn't work for internal models where there can be non-contiguous input tensors:

- size=[8192, 16416], stride=[16448, 1]  # stride[0] is larger than size[1]
- size=[1152, 384], stride=[1, 1152]  # column-major tensor

In this PR, we relax the assumption on contiguous input tensor, by switching from `.view()` to `.reshape()`. Note that since `.reshape()` will try to use `.view()` under the hood whenever possible, this should not cause regression to existing use cases.

Looking at the code changes, I can see this is a bug fix in the `deepspeed/runtime/zero/tiling.py` file. The change modifies the `forward` method in what appears to be a tiling/splitting utility class.

The key change is:
- Previously, the code used `self.in_parts` (which was likely computed during `__init__` and stored as an instance variable)
- Now, it computes `input_parts` dynamically from the actual input shape using `partition(input_.shape[-1], self.in_splits)`

This fixes a bug where the split sizes were being calculated from stale/partition sizes stored at initialization time (`self.in_parts`), rather than from the actual current input tensor dimensions. The fix ensures the split sizes are computed dynamically based on the actual input shape, which is important when input tensor dimensions may vary (e.g., with dynamic shapes).

Based on the reference examples and the nature of the change, this is a fix type commit.

fix(runtime/zero): Fix dynamic shape handling in tiling split computation

The forward method was using pre-computed partition sizes (`self.in_parts`) from initialization to calculate split sizes. This caused incorrect behavior when input tensor dimensions differ from the initial shape (e.g., with dynamic shapes or varying batch sizes).

Compute `input_parts` dynamically from the actual input shape using `partition(input_.shape[-1], self.in_splits)` instead of relying on cached `self.in_parts`. This ensures correct splitting behavior regardless of input tensor dimensions.
messages.claude:
fix: use correct partition boundaries when splitting non-default inputs in TiledLinear

When `in_splits > 1` and the input was not already split, the forward
pass computed per-partition split sizes by diffing `self.in_parts`,
which holds the partition boundaries for the *configured* (default)
input shape. If the actual `input_` tensor has a different last-dim
size, those boundaries no longer line up with the tensor, producing
incorrect (or negative) split sizes and corrupting the resulting
chunks.

- Compute `input_parts` from the real input shape via
  `partition(input_.shape[-1], self.in_splits)` so the split sizes
  match the tensor being split.
- Add a blank line for readability in `split_tensor_along_last_dim`.

Why: `self.in_parts` is cached for the configured input shape and is
only valid when `input_` matches that shape. For inputs whose last
dimension differs from the configured one, reusing `self.in_parts`
caused splits to be computed against stale boundaries, leading to
runtime errors or silently wrong partitions. Recomputing the
boundaries from the actual input shape keeps the split correct across
varying input widths.
messages.minimax:
fix: use actual input shape for split sizes instead of cached in_parts

The original code used `self.in_parts` (cached partition boundaries) to calculate split sizes, which could be incorrect if the actual input shape differs from what was expected when `in_parts` was computed. Changed to compute `input_parts` fresh from `input_.shape[-1]` before calculating split sizes, ensuring splits match the actual input dimensions.

Replace PyTorch's `ctx.save_for_backward()` with a custom `ctx.deepspeed_saved_tensors` attribute in the activation checkpointing module. This change avoids conflicts with PyTorch's internal backward tensor management while maintaining the same functionality for storing and retrieving tensors during the backward pass. The modification ensures compatibility with DeepSpeed's custom checkpointing logic and prevents potential issues with tensor lifecycle management in distributed training scenarios.
messages.minimax:
fix: rename saved_tensors to avoid conflict with PyTorch autograd

Rename `ctx.saved_tensors` to `ctx.deepspeed_saved_tensors` in activation checkpointing to avoid naming conflict with PyTorch's autograd `ctx.saved_tensors`. Also add `print_backward_tensors` debug utility function for inspecting gradient tensors in backward pass.
messages.claude:
fix: avoid saving activation checkpoint tensors via ctx.save_for_backward to prevent backward graph retention

What:
- Replace ctx.save_for_backward(*tensor_args) with ctx.deepspeed_saved_tensors = tensor_args in checkpointing.py forward()
- Update backward() to read from ctx.deepspeed_saved_tensors across all three code paths (PARTITION_ACTIVATIONS, CPU_CHECKPOINT, and default)
- Add new print_backward_tensors debug helper in deepspeed/utils/debug.py that walks grad_fn.next_functions to print tensor id/shape/data/grad

Why:
torch.autograd's ctx.save_for_backward is intended for tensors that need gradients. When activation checkpointing saves the full forward input tensors through it, autograd retains references that keep the backward graph (and its intermediate tensors) alive across the forward pass. This defeats the memory savings that activation checkpointing is supposed to provide, since the very tensors we are trying to free are held alive until backward() runs.

By storing the checkpointed tensors on a plain attribute (ctx.deepspeed_saved_tensors) instead of through save_for_backward, we avoid tying their lifetime to the autograd graph. This lets the framework release the saved activations when appropriate and only materialize them again at backward time, restoring the expected memory behavior of activation checkpointing. The three backward() call sites are updated correspondingly so they consume the new attribute rather than ctx.saved_tensors.

The new print_backward_tensors utility in debug.py is added to help inspect the backward graph and confirm which tensors are retained, aiding diagnosis of residual memory retention issues during checkpointed backward passes.

* Major rework of `optree_impl` and `dmtree_impl` for consistency. (#20481)

The `optree` implementation and the `dmtree` implementation of the `tree` API had a nummber of discreptancies. Running unit tests without `optree` installed would fail on a number of tests.

The documentation and behavior of the `tree` API was not internally consistent. There was contradicting documentation about the handling of `OrderedDict`s. The behavior of the `optree` implementation was to use the key sorted order for `pack_sequence_as` but use the sequence order for `flatten`, resulting in `flatten` + `pack_sequence_as` not being idempotent (as discovered in https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/20538 )

The exceptions used to report non-matching structures where different between the two implementation. When `optree` uses `ValueError` for all mimatches, `dmtree` would distinguish between `ValueError` and `TypeError` for some cases. This caused a number of bugs because `TypeError` was often not caught, only `ValueError`.

The `assert_same_structure` argument of `check_types` is deprecated and no longer does anything. The `optree` implementation would check the types of the *leaves*, whereas the `dmtree` would check the types of the *collections*. So `check_types=False` with `optree` was fairly, although not completely similar, to `check_types=True` with `dmtree`. The rules is that no two collection types are considered the same, except for `dict`, `OrderedDict` and `defaultdict`.

Because `optree` is the default implementation used and `dmtree` is only a fallback, this PR changes the `tree` API behavior to conform to the `optree` approach everywhere. This makes the `optree` implementation a thin wrapper on top of `optree`, whereas large portions of the `dmtree` wrapper are now reimplemented in Python. Note that the `tree` API was initially modelled after `dmtree`, not `optree`.

There are a couple of fairly niche known discrepancies between the `optree` implementation and the `dmtree` implementation. They are documented in `dmtree_impl.py`.

- Fixed references to `unflatten_as` in documentation, which doesn't exist.
- Fixed contradicting documentation in `flatten` and `pack_sequence_as` related to the handling of `OrderedDict`s. The documentation now states that the sequence order is always used.
- Made handling of `OrderedDict`s follow the spec with both `optree` and `dmtree`.
- Made the exceptions raised consistent and documented them. `TypeError` is only for major programmer error (e.g. `func` is not callable), and `ValueError` is used for all structure mismatches.
- Removed all cases where `TypeError` was caught after a `assert_same_structure`.
- Fixed the discrepancy in the behavior for `namedtuple`s. The `optree` behavior is now followed, meaning that the path for fields are indices, not field names.
- Deprecated the `check_types` argument in `assert_same_structure` and implemented the `optree` behavior in `dmtree`.
- Remove `sequence_fn` argument of `pack_sequence_as`, which was not used and force the `optree` implementation to be fully rewritten in Python.
- Added `MAP_TO_NONE` to the API, added support for it in both implementations of `traverse`. This feature was documented, but not accessible and not actually implemented.
- Added support for registered classes with `dmtree`, both with `flatten` and `unflatten` passed at registration time and methods on the class.
- Tracked collections are now supported with `dmtree` (`TrackedList`, `TrackedSet` and `TrackedDict`). In particular, `TrackedSet` would be handled as a leaf and never traversed.
- Removed dependency of tracked collections on `optree` in `tree_flatten` and `tree_unflatten`.
- Tensorflow's `ListWrapper` and `_DictWrapper` are now supported with `dmtree`.
- Implemented a more efficient way for `optree` to verify structures are the same while traversing them with `map_structure` and `map_structure_up_to`. This avoids multiple traversals.
- Added documentation for `list_to_tuples` and `map_shape_structure`.
- Completely rewrote all tree API unit tests, which are now painfully thorough.
- `map_shape_structure` is now unit tested.
- Fixed unintented use of `tree` instead of `keras.tree` in unit test.
- Ran unit tests for all backends with `optree` uninstalled.

* Fix recurrent dropout for GRU. (#20656)

The simplified implementation, which used the same recurrent dropout masks for all the previous states didn't work and caused the training to not converge with large enough recurrent dropout values.

This new implementation is now the same as Keras 2. Note that recurrent dropout requires "implementation 1" to be turned on.

Fixes https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/20276

* Fix example title in probabilistic_metrics.py (#20662)

* Change recurrent dropout implementation for LSTM. (#20663)

This change is to make the implementation of recurrent dropout consistent with GRU (changed as of https://github.com/keras-team/keras/pull/20656 ) and Keras 2.

Also fixed a bug where the GRU fix would break when using CUDNN with a dropout and no recurrent dropout. The solution is to create multiple masks only when needed (implementation == 1).

Added coverage for the case when dropout is set and recurrent dropout is not set.

* Never pass enable_xla=False or native_serialization=False in tests (#20664)

These are invalid options in the latest version of jax2tf, they
will just immediately throw.

* Fix `PyDatasetAdapterTest::test_class_weight` test with Torch on GPU. (#20665)

The test was failing because arrays on device and on cpu were compared.

* Fix up torch GPU failing test for mix up (#20666)

We need to make sure to use get any tensors places on cpu before using
them in the tensorflow backend during preprocessing.

* Specify window_length dtype requirement in tf.keras.ops.istft in math.py (#20728)

The `window_length` parameter in `tf.keras.ops.istft` requires `tf.int32` dtype, but this isn't documented. This can cause unexpected `ValueError` when using `tf.int64` and `tf.int16`

Here is the Example case:
```
import tensorflow as tf

input_dict = {
    'stfts': tf.constant([[-0.87817144+1.14583987j, -0.32066484+0.25565411j]], dtype=tf.complex128),
    'frame_length': tf.constant(256, dtype=tf.int16),
    'frame_step': tf.constant(5120,dtype=tf.int64)
}
result = tf.signal.inverse_stft(**input_dict)
print(result)
```
The code throws the following error:
```
ValueError: window_length: Tensor conversion requested dtype int32 for Tensor with dtype int64
```

* fix(ops): Fix inconsistent padding calculation in PyTorch backend ops

Was able to still reproduce the error, the PyTorch backend had inconsistent
behavior between static shape inference and dynamic execution for pooling
operations, particularly with 'same' padding and non-unit strides, figured
that the root cause was by incorrect padding calculation logic that didn't
properly handle asymmetric padding cases.

Key changes:
- Rewrote _compute_padding_length() to handle stride-based padding
- Fixed padding calculation to properly support asymmetric padding cases
- Standardize channels_first/channels_last conversion in pooling ops
- Cleaned up padding application in _apply_same_padding()
- Added proper handling of data_format throughout pooling pipeline

This fixes the issue where MaxPooling2D with 'same' padding would produce
different shapes between compute_output_shape() and actual execution
(e.g. (1,5,2,2) vs (1,5,2,1)).

fix: correct largest partitioned param numel calculation and remove dead _create_fp16_partitions code

What:
- In `stage3.py`, fix the computation of `largest_partitioned_param_numel` so it takes the max of both `tensor.numel()` and `tensor.ds_numel` for each tensor in the fp16 partitioned groups, ensuring the largest partitioned parameter size is measured correctly.
- Remove the now-unused `_create_fp16_partitions` method from `ZeroStage3`, as this logic is no longer invoked (fp16 partition creation is handled elsewhere).

Why:
The previous calculation only considered `tensor.numel()`, which underestimates the true size of partitioned parameters when `ds_tensor`/`ds_numel` semantics apply. Using `ds_numel` ensures the reported largest partitioned param numel reflects the actual sharded tensor size used by DeepSpeed's zero stage 3, which is critical for downstream buffer allocation and memory planning decisions. Removing the dead `_create_fp16_partitions` method cleans up code that has been superseded by the current partitioning path, reducing maintenance burden and avoiding confusion about which code path is authoritative.

Also removed the redundant `_create_fp16_partitions` function as its functionality has been consolidated into `_move_to_flat_buffer`.

fix: handle contiguous gradients in ZeRO stage 1

Summary: Add missing handling for contiguous gradients in ZeRO stage 1 optimizer state partitioning. Previously, when using ZeRO stage 1 (optimizer state partitioning only), the `copy_grads_in_partition` method was not being called for gradients when `contiguous_gradients` was enabled, unlike in stage 2.

Why: In ZeRO stage 2, gradients are partitioned across data parallel ranks, and the code correctly handled copying gradients into the partition when `contiguous_gradients` is True. However, in stage 1 where only optimizer states are partitioned (not gradients), the else branch was missing the contiguous gradients handling. This caused gradients to not be properly copied into the contiguous buffer, potentially leading to memory inefficiencies or incorrect gradient accumulation behavior when using stage 1 with contiguous gradients enabled.

was never called, leaving the partition buffer unpopulated and causing
incorrect gradient reduction. Add the else branch to handle stage 1 by
copying grads into the partition buffer when contiguous_gradients is set.

[CI] Keep going display on HUD: upload log when test fails (#155371)

I guess this is more of an RFC

Goal:
Enable keep going so that we can get information immediately for failures.  We want be aware of failures as soon as possible, especially on the main branch, this is so that reverts can happen quickly.

Proposal:
A job with `keep-going` will continue through errors in `python run_test.py`.  If a test fails, before it runs the next test, it will upload a fake log that should have enough information in it so that viewing the log will be able to tell you what failed and any stack traces/error logs, and should be able to be parsed by log classifier to get a line.

I am getting the log by concating the test logs in test/test-reports, which is all the text outputted by pytest (unless someone runs with `ci-verbose-test-logs` label).  There are obviously many things this won't catch, ex output outside of run_test.py, some output inside of run_test.py, but it should be enough.

After a log finishes, eventually its raw log is uploaded to ossci-raw-job-status s3 bucket and the log classifier will read it to do classification.  This means we will have to change log classifier to read from this bucket as well.
I'm thinking just add an input parameter to log classifier like https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/6723/files
Also upload the temp results to a temp attribute instead of the real one

To overwrite the conclusion on HUD, I'm thinking a lambda that is s3 put trigger on the fake log being put into s3, that does something similar to log classifier where it just mutates the entry https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/blob/13a990b6787cf19f87cc51381c3f151c6767f2b6/aws/lambda/log-classifier/src/network.rs#L85 to add a new field like "will_fail": true, and also triggers the log classifier to run

Then we change HUD/ClickHouse to point the raw log url to the alternate place, the new "will_fail" field as the conclusion, and the temp log classifier result if needed

Why always write to temp attribution/column? I am unsure about overwriting the real results with fake ones

Pros:
Not many changes outside of HUD/UI

Cons:
Lots of moving parts, lots of temp fields that will require adjustment for queries, temp fields never really get deleted

messages.kimi:
1. Code Changes Analysis:
   - In `deepspeed/runtime/engine.py`: Added calls to `checkpoint_event_prologue()` and `checkpoint_event_epilogue()` in the `load_checkpoint` method, similar to how they're used in `save_checkpoint`
   - In `deepspeed/runtime/zero/stage3.py`: 
     - Modified `release_and_reset_all()` to take a `module` parameter and use `iter_params(module, recurse=True)` instead of `self.__param_order`
     - Renamed `save_checkpoint_prologue/epilogue` to `checkpoint_event_prologue/epilogue` to make them generic for both save and load operations
   - In `tests/unit/test_checkpointing.py`: Added two new test cases `test_immediate_save_load` and `test_load_immediate_save` that test checkpoint operations across all zero stages

2. The "Why":
   - The issue being fixed is that when loading a checkpoint with ZeRO-3, parameters need to be properly partitioned before the load operation (similar to how save works)
   - The rename from `save_checkpoint_*` to `checkpoint_event_*` indicates these methods are now being reused for both save and load checkpoint events
   - The tests verify that immediate save/load and load/immediate-save operations work correctly across all ZeRO stages

3. Commit Type:
   - This is a fix - it's fixing a bug where checkpoint loading wasn't properly handling parameter partitioning in ZeRO-3

Based on the reference examples and the pattern of explaining both technical details and rationale:

fix: Ensure proper parameter partitioning during checkpoint load in ZeRO-3

The checkpoint loading path was missing the parameter partitioning preparation
that exists for checkpoint saving. When using ZeRO-3 optimization, parameters
must be partitioned before checkpoint operations to ensure correct state
management. Without this fix, loading a checkpoint immediately after saving
(or vice versa) could fail due to parameters not being in the expected
partitioned state.

This change:
1. Adds checkpoint_event_prologue/epilogue calls to load_checkpoint(), similar
   to the existing save_checkpoint() implementation
2. Renames save_checkpoint_prologue/epilogue to checkpoint_event_prologue/epilogue
   to reflect their dual use for both save and load operations
3. Updates release_and_reset_all() to accept a module parameter for proper
   parameter iteration during checkpoint events
4. Adds test coverage for immediate save/load and load/immediate-save scenarios
   across all ZeRO stages (0-3)
messages.claude:
fix: ensure all parameters are partitioned before checkpoint load

What:
- Add `checkpoint_event_prologue()`/`checkpoint_event_epilogue()` calls around the load path in `engine.load_checkpoint` so that ZeRO-3 parameters are partitioned before state-dict restore and restored afterwards, mirroring what already happens on the save path.
- Rename `save_checkpoint_prologue/epilogue` to `checkpoint_event_prologue/epilogue` in `stage3.py` to reflect that the hooks now serve both save and load.
- Update `release_and_reset_all` to take an explicit `module` argument and iterate parameters via `iter_params(module, recurse=True)` instead of relying on the internal `__param_order` trace, so partitioning works even when the trace has not been populated (e.g. immediately after engine init).
- Update the only internal caller `_partition_all_parameters` to pass `self.module`.
- Add `test_immediate_save_load` and `test_load_immediate_save` covering save/load and load/save sequences at ZeRO stages 0-3 with no training step in between.

Why:
ZeRO stage 3 lazily partitions parameters, relying on forward/backward hooks to drive partitioning. When a checkpoint is saved or loaded immediately after engine construction (before any forward pass), the `__param_order` trace is empty, so `release_and_reset_all` released no parameters and `_partition_all_parameters` left parameters in an unpartitioned state. This caused the saved/loaded state dict to contain full gathered weights rather than partitioned shards, corrupting the checkpoint for stage 3 and crashing on the load-then-save round trip. Routing the prologue/epilogue through both save and load, and iterating the live module tree instead of the stale trace, ensures parameters are consistently partitioned for any checkpoint event regardless of prior forward/backward activity.
messages.minimax:
fix: add missing checkpoint_event_prologue/epilogue calls in load_checkpoint for zero optimization

When loading a checkpoint with zero_optimization_partition_weights enabled, the parameter partitioning was not being properly managed. This caused issues particularly when loading immediately after saving, as parameters remained in an inconsistent state.

The save path already correctly called checkpoint_event_prologue/epilogue around the save operation, but the load path was missing these calls entirely. Additionally, the prologue/epilogue methods were renamed from save_checkpoint_prologue/save_checkpoint_epilogue to checkpoint_event_prologue/checkpoint_event_epilogue to reflect their dual use for both save and load operations.

The release_and_reset_all method was also fixed to accept a module parameter and use iter_params(module, recurse=True) for correct parameter iteration, ensuring parameters are properly released before partitioning during checkpoint operations.

messages.claude:
feat: split PartitionedParameterCoordinator into separate training/eval instances

Extracts PartitionedParameterCoordinator into its own module and introduces a
_get_param_coordinator(training) factory that maintains distinct coordinators
for training vs. inference/eval modes.

Previously, a single param_coordinator was shared across forward, backward, and
evaluation passes. During eval-only forward passes (torch._C.is_grad_enabled()
== False), reset_step was called at the end of the forward hook, which discarded
the training trace accumulated during the actual training step. This caused
tracing state to be repeatedly invalidated and broke the prefetch ordering
established for the training pass.

By keying coordinators on the training flag, the training trace stays intact
across interleaved evaluation/inference calls, while eval gets its own
independent trace and prefetch queue. record_trace is also moved to run alongside
release_sub_module in the post-forward/backward hooks so tracing completes
correctly for both modes.

Also moves tracing bookkeeping (record_trace/reset_step) out of the engine's
forward path and into the coordinator hooks, and adds nvme prefetch support via
the prefetch_nvme flag.
messages.minimax:
fix: separate ZeRO-3 param coordinators for training vs eval modes

The previous implementation used a single param coordinator that was incorrectly reset during evaluation, causing issues when switching between training and eval modes. This commit introduces separate `PartitionedParameterCoordinator` instances for training and non-training modes, managed via `_get_param_coordinator(training)` to ensure parameter state is not polluted between modes.

The change fixes issues where evaluation mode (no gradients) would interfere with the training trace state, as the old code would reset the step when `torch._C.is_grad_enabled()` was False, which could disrupt ongoing training traces.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix param release logic when prefetcher skips AVAILABLE params

The prefetcher skips AVAILABLE params when scanning the param trace, which causes two issues: (1) performance degradation because skipped uses are never prefetched, and (2) swap buffer exhaustion for NVMe params because the prefetch order diverges from the trace. Fix by preventing release of params whose reuse was skipped by prefetch, detected by checking if the most recent step ID fetched for a param exceeds the current step ID. Also includes minor logging improvements (reduce swap statistics from INFO to DEBUG level) and test updates to properly validate prefetching behavior with configurable bucket sizes.
messages.minimax:
fix: prevent early param release when prefetch skips reuse

When the prefetcher scans the param trace, it skips AVAILABLE params, causing
two problems: (1) skipped uses are never prefetched, hurting performance, and
(2) for nvme params the prefetch order diverges from the trace, leading to swap
buffer exhaustion.

Fix by not releasing params whose reuse was skipped by prefetch - detected via
most_recent_step_id_param_fetched_for tracking. Also fix an off-by-one in the
reuse distance check (>= instead of >).
messages.claude:
fix: prevent prefetcher from releasing params whose reuse was skipped

The partitioned param coordinator's __params_to_release logic did not
account for params whose reuse the prefetcher skipped when scanning the
param trace. When such params were released before their next (skipped)
use, two problems arose:

1. Performance regression: skipped uses were never prefetched, so they
   had to be fetched synchronously at use time.
2. Buffer exhaustion for nvme params: the prefetch order diverged from
   the recorded trace, causing swap-in buffers to run out.

The prefetcher now records the most recent step id it fetched each param
for. When deciding which params to release, we discard any param whose
recorded fetch step id is greater than the current step id, so it stays
available for its upcoming skipped reuse.

Additional changes support the fix:
- async_swapper: lower swap statistics logging from info to debug to
  reduce log noise during prefetch-heavy runs.
- partitioned_param_swapper: extend the "Num available" debug print to
  include param ids, aiding diagnosis of prefetch/buffer divergence.
- partitioned_param_coordinator: also fix the reuse-distance boundary
  check from > to >= so a param reused at exactly
  __max_reuse_dist_in_numel is preserved.
- test_zero: split the combined `prefetching` flag into
  `use_module_trace` and `param_prefetching` so prefetch behavior can be
  exercised independently of module tracing, and add a prefetching
  parametrize dimension with a prefetch_bucket_size sized to all params.

Based on the code changes, I can see this is fixing a bug where `communication_data_type` was being passed as a parameter but should instead use `self.communication_data_type` from the class instance. The fix ensures proper dtype handling in ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3, with corresponding tests added.

fix: Use self.communication_data_type instead of hardcoded parameter in ZeRO allreduce operations

The allreduce_bucket method in ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3 was accepting communication_data_type as a parameter defaulting to torch.float16, but this ignored the configured communication_data_type setting. This caused incorrect dtype conversions during gradient reduction when users specified a different communication dtype (e.g., bf16) than the default fp16.

The fix removes the communication_data_type parameter from allreduce_bucket signatures and instead uses self.communication_data_type consistently. For average_tensor in stage 1 and 2, we now properly convert tensors to the configured communication dtype before reduction and copy back afterwards, matching the behavior in stage3. This ensures gradient allreduce operations respect the user's communication_data_type configuration across all ZeRO stages.

Tests added to verify correct dtype handling for various combinations of computation and communication dtypes.
messages.claude:
fix: respect communication_data_type config in ZeRO allreduce and average_tensor

Currently, allreduce_bucket hardcodes the default communication_data_type
to torch.float16, ignoring the user's "communication_data_type" config
unless pg_correctness_test forces fp32. This makes the dtype-cocktail
config (e.g. fp16 params with bfp16 comms) silently fall back to fp16
and produce numerically wrong reductions.

Why:
- ZeRO Stage 1/2/3 should honor the configured comm dtype so that users
  can mix compute and communication precisions (e.g. bfloat16 compute
  with fp16 comms, or fp32 compute with bfp16 comms) as documented.
- In stage_1_and_2.average_tensor, the tensor sent to reduce must be
  cast to communication_data_type before slicing into per-rank buckets,
  otherwise the reduce op runs on the compute dtype rather than the
  requested comm dtype. After reduce, copy the reduced buffer back so
  the original gradient tensor retains the compute dtype for subsequent
  accumulation.
- The new test_zero_dtype_cocktail unit test monkeypatches dist.reduce
  to assert the reduced tensor dtype matches comm_torch_dtype across
  all six compute/comm dtype combinations, locking in this behavior.

Changes:
- deepspeed/runtime/zero/stage3.py: drop hardcoded float16 default from
  allreduce_bucket; use self.communication_data_type when not in
  pg_correctness_test.
- deepspeed/runtime/zero/stage_1_and_2.py: same allreduce_bucket fix,
  and cast tensor_to_reduce to communication_data_type before narrowing
  into grad slices, restoring the original dtype after reduction.
- tests/unit/test_bf16.py: add test_zero_dtype_cocktail parametrized
  over six (compute, comm) dtype combinations.

Cast to unsigned char to avoid UB (#152360)

The standard requires that the argument to functions like `isdigit`, `isalpha`, and similar must be either `EOF` or an `unsigned char`; otherwise, the behavior is undefined (UB).
To avoid out-of-bounds reads, modern implementations of some libraries (such as glibc) deliberately pad their internal tables to guarantee valid memory access even for negative values. However, this is implementation-specific, and other libraries may not do this.

Properly casting the argument to `unsigned char` is good practice to avoid potential issues on some platforms.

Enable keep going so that we can get information immediately for failures.  We want be aware of failures as soon as possible, especially on the main branch, this is so that reverts can happen quickly.

Summary:

However this alone is not satisfactory: the exported program by design has only one graph, representing one path through the model, and we cannot necessarily guarantee that this graph works for the additional example inputs because different guards might have been created if we had exported with them instead (corresponding to different traced paths). However, checking that the additional example inputs satisfy the guards created by the original export should be sufficient for generalization.

- Extend `zero_to_fp32.py` to merge frozen params back when reconstructing the fp32 state dict, and refactor `parse_model_state` into `parse_model_states` returning a `zero_model_state` dataclass
- Adapt pipeline engine's `load_module_state_dict` override to the new `checkpoint`-based signature
- Add `SimpleFrozenModel` and new test cases covering frozen-param save/load and load-module-only flows

Why:
ZeRO stage 1/2/3 partitions optimizer state across ranks, but frozen (requires_grad=False) parameters are not owned by the optimizer and were therefore silently dropped from checkpoints. This made it impossible to correctly restore models with mixed trainable/frozen weights (e.g. partial fine-tuning of pretrained backbones), and broke `zero_to_fp32` reconstruction since frozen tensors were missing from the recovered state dict. By persisting frozen param fragments alongside param_shapes and rehydrating them on load (via `ds_tensor` for partitioned params or direct copy otherwise), mixed trainability models now round-trip correctly through save/load. The bf16_optimizer filter also prevents frozen params from being incorrectly accumulated into trainable bf16 flat groups.

messages.claude:
feat: add bfloat16 support to FusedAdam optimizer

This change extends FusedAdam to support bfloat16 (bf16) parameters, which was previously limited to fp16 and fp32. As mixed-precision training with bf16 becomes more prevalent (especially on Ampere+ GPUs where bf16 offers wider dynamic range than fp16 without loss scaling), FusedAdam users were unable to leverage bf16 parameters without falling back to unfused or fp32 paths, negating the performance benefits of the fused kernel.

The implementation adds a dedicated bf16 tensor group (g_bf, p_bf, m_bf, v_bf) alongside the existing fp16 and fp32 groups, routing bf16 params through multi_tensor_adam with the same update logic. The error message for unsupported dtypes is updated accordingly, and the empty-param-group case is now skipped to avoid unnecessary kernel launches.

feat: Add safe accessor functions for ZeRO optimizer parameters and gradients

Add safe_get_full_fp32_param, safe_get_full_grad, and safe_get_full_optimizer_state utility functions to enable safe access to full high-precision parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across all ZeRO stages (1, 2, 3) and bf16_optimizer. This addresses the need for external tools and callbacks to inspect optimizer state without directly accessing internal data structures that vary across ZeRO implementations.

The changes include:
- New accessor functions in tensor_fragment.py that handle the differences between ZeRO stages
- Enhanced link_hp_params to track gradient dictionaries and parameter indices
- Added _link_all_hp_params to stage3.py to establish parameter-to-optimizer mapping

messages.minimax:
feat: add APIs to retrieve full fp32 gradients and optimizer states from fragmented params

This commit adds the ability to access full high-precision (fp32) gradients and optimizer states from low-precision (fp16/bf16) parameter fragments in ZeRO optimization. Previously, retrieving the complete fp32 gradient required manual reconstruction across partitions. The new API provides `safe_get_full_grad()`, `safe_get_full_fp32_param()`, and `safe_get_full_optimizer_state()` functions that handle the reconstruction automatically across all ZeRO stages (1, 2, 3) and the bf16_optimizer, supporting both GPU and offload (cpu/nvme) configurations. A new test suite validates that all tensor fragments can be correctly reassembled to their full hp forms.
messages.claude:
feat: add unified APIs to gather full fp32 params, gradients, and optimizer states across ZeRO stages

What:
- Add safe_get_full_fp32_param, safe_get_full_grad, and safe_get_full_optimizer_state helpers in deepspeed/utils/tensor_fragment.py that work uniformly for ZeRO stage 1/2/3 and bf16_optimizer params.
- Implement get_full_hp_grad for stage 1/2 and get_fp32_grad_for_param / get_full_hp_param for stage 3, including _fp32_state_allgather to reconstruct the full tensor across the data-parallel group.
- Thread gradient_dict / offload_gradient_dict / use_offload / param_group_index through link_hp_params and tensor_fragment so low-precision params can locate their fp32 gradient fragment (CPU offload or GPU resident).
- Attach _z3_optimizer to every module parameter in stage3 so stage-3 params can be identified via ds_id and routed to the stage-3 APIs.
- Clear param.grad for empty gradient partitions in stage3.__partition_grads to avoid stale gradients being exposed to the new gather API.
- Add unit test tests/unit/runtime/zero/test_zero_tensor_fragment.py covering stages 1/2/3 with none/cpu/nvme offload plus bf16, and relax bf16_required_version_check with an accelerator_check flag so bf16 tests can run without native HW bf16.

Why:
Users (and downstream tooling such as TensorBoard) previously had no portable way to inspect the full fp32 master weights, gradients, or optimizer states for a sharded parameter — each ZeRO stage and the bf16 optimizer stored these tensors differently and exposed no common accessor. This blocked debugging, custom optimizer integration, and gradient/weight introspection workflows.

The new safe_get_* APIs provide a single entry point that dispatches based on param attributes (ds_id vs _hp_mapping), so callers can retrieve the assembled fp32 tensor without knowing which ZeRO stage is active. The gradient path also raises a clear error when gradients are not currently materialized (i.e., outside the backward-to-step window), preventing silent misuse. The accompanying tests validate the API across all stages and offload devices, including frozen-weight handling.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix device placement and broadcast for ZeRO-3 models

The changes fix two issues with ZeRO-3 model initialization:

1. Device placement: Previously, the engine would move the model to the target device even when using ZeRO-3, which uses `zero.Init()` to handle device placement. This caused unnecessary device transfers and potential issues with partitioned parameters. The fix adds `is_zero3_model` check to skip device placement for ZeRO-3 models.

2. Model broadcast: The `_broadcast_model()` call was being executed for ZeRO-3 models, which is redundant since ZeRO-3 handles parameter distribution through its own partitioning mechanism. The fix excludes ZeRO-3 models from the broadcast step.

Additionally, the change refactors the ZeRO-3 detection logic by extracting the repeated `zero_optimization_partition_weights()` and `ds_id` attribute checks into a single `is_zero3_model` variable for cleaner code.
messages.minimax:
fix: skip device placement and broadcast for ZeRO-3 models

ZeRO-3 partitioned models are already placed on devices by zero.Init() during
partitioning. Calling module.to() after zero.Init() is redundant and can cause
device mismatch. Similarly, _broadcast_model() interferes with ZeRO-3's
parameter synchronization. This fixes crashes and incorrect behavior when
using FP16/BF16 precision with ZeRO-3 partitioning.
messages.claude:
fix: skip manual device placement and broadcast for zero3-initialized models

What:
- Hoist the zero3 detection check (`zero_optimization_partition_weights()` and
  params with `ds_id`) into a single `is_zero3_model` variable in
  `_configure_distributed_model`.
- Reuse it for the fp16/bfloat16 param dtype validation branches (no behavior change).
- Skip `self.module.to(self.device)` when `is_zero3_model` is true, since
  `zero.Init()` already handles device placement of the model.
- Skip `self._broadcast_model()` when `is_zero3_model` is true, since the model
  is already partitioned/initialized through the zero3 path.

Why:
For zero3 models, parameters are managed by DeepSpeed's `zero.Init()` context,
which owns their device placement and sharding. Forcing `module.to(self.device)`
and a full `_broadcast_model()` afterwards is both redundant and incorrect:
- `module.to(self.device)` can cigger the zero3 partitioning state and trigger
  spurious materialization of parameters that should stay partitioned.
- `_broadcast_model()` broadcasts the full model across ranks, which defeats the
  memory savings of zero3 partitioning and can corrupt the already-initialized
  partitioned parameters.

By gating both operations on `not is_zero3_model`, we let zero3 retain
ownership of model initialization while preserving the existing fp16/bfloat16
param-check behavior. Consolidating the repeated zero3 condition into
`is_zero3_model` also improves readability and keeps the three call sites in
sync.

workflow files under `.github/workflows/`.

recommended version with improved Node.js runtime, better support for
modern runner environments, and ongoing security maintenance. Keeping
the checkout action on a supported version ensures CI pipelines continue
to receive bug fixes and avoids potential deprecation warnings or future
breakage as v2 approaches end-of-life.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add `empty_partition_cache` API for explicit GPU memory cleanup in ZeRO-3

Add `empty_partition_cache()` method to DeepSpeedEngine to allow users to explicitly release GPU memory consumed by offloaded model parameters after training. By default, ZeRO-3 keeps parameters unpartitioned at the end of training as an optimization for potential training resumption. This new API provides a way to clear cached parameters when the memory is needed for other purposes, such as inference or subsequent training jobs.

The implementation adds the method across the engine hierarchy:
- `DeepSpeedEngine.empty_partition_cache()` - public API that triggers cleanup
- `DeepSpeedZeroOptimizer_Stage3.empty_partition_cache()` - delegates to parameter offload
- `DeepSpeedZeRoOffload.empty_partition_cache()` - calls `partition_all_parameters()` to move parameters back to CPU/offloaded storage

Also includes a minor fix changing the persistence threshold check from `<` to `<=` for consistent boundary behavior, and adds comprehensive unit tests verifying the cache clearing functionality in both training and non-training modes.
messages.claude:
feat: add empty_partition_cache for ZeRO-3 to release GPU memory

Add a DeepSpeedEngine.empty_partition_cache() method that walks through
the ZeRO stage-3 optimizer and parameter_offload layers to re-partition
parameters left unpartitioned at the end of training. Persistent params
are kept unpartitioned on purpose as an optimization for resuming
training, which means they continue to hold GPU memory after the loop
exits. This new API gives users an explicit way to free that memory via
gc.collect() + accelerator.empty_cache().

Also fix mark_persistent_parameters to use param.ds_numel <= param_threshold
so parameters exactly at the threshold qualify as persistent, matching the
documented semantics of stage3_param_persistence_threshold.

Docs and a DistributedTest (TestZeroPartitionCache) are added to cover both
training and inference paths.
messages.minimax:
feat: Add empty_partition_cache method to release GPU memory in ZeRO-3

After training with ZeRO stage 3, some parameters remain unpartitioned and use GPU memory as an optimization for faster resumption. This commit adds an `empty_partition_cache()` method that explicitly releases GPU memory consumed by partitioned parameters, giving users control over when to free this memory. The method delegates to the optimizer's offload subsystem and triggers garbage collection and accelerator cache clearing. Documentation and tests are included.
